# The conceptual leap {.unnumbered}

## What this note assumes

This is a broad conceptual note about random probability measures, not merely
a Walker companion. It can be read in layers:

- For Sections [The two measurable spaces](#rpm-two-spaces) through
  [The notation at the two levels](#rpm-two-level-notation), read
  [sets and pushforwards](sets-functions-and-pushforwards.qmd) and
  [measure foundations](measure-probability-foundations.qmd).
- Before [Densities versus probability measures](#rpm-densities-vs-measures),
  use the [density guide](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd#absolute-continuity-is-a-relationship-between-measures)
  if domination and $dG/d\lambda$ are unfamiliar.
- Before the [finite random-measure example](#rpm-finite-example) and
  [Dirichlet process](#rpm-dirichlet-process), read the
  [Dirac measure definition](dirac-measure-and-dirac-delta.qmd#the-dirac-probability-measure).
- The separate [Bayesian notation guide](../Bayesian/bayes-measure-d-concept.qmd#notation-prior-on-densities)
  is needed only when connecting this object to $\Pi(df\mid X)$ and Bayes'
  rule.

No stochastic-process or topology course is assumed. The note supplies enough
of those ideas to understand random measures, while marking proof-level theory
as optional.

An ordinary probability distribution assigns probabilities to events in a data
space. A Bayesian nonparametric prior assigns probabilities to **sets of
probability distributions**.

Using $\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ for the set of probability measures on the data
space,

$$
G\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X),
\qquad
\Pi\in\mathcal P\{\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\}.
$$

The two symbols live at different levels:

- $G$ assigns probability to data-space events;
- $\Pi$ assigns probability to sets of candidate $G$'s.

This two-level construction explains how a distribution itself can be random.

In this note, $\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ means **probability measures on
$\mathcal X$**, not the power set of $\mathcal X$. Both conventions occur in
mathematics, so always check the author's definition.

# The two measurable spaces {#rpm-two-spaces}

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathscr X)$ be the data space. Define

$$
\mathcal P(\mathcal X)
=\{G:G\text{ is a probability measure on }(\mathcal X,\mathscr X)\}.
$$

To put a probability law on this set, it also needs a sigma-field. A natural
choice is the **evaluation sigma-field**, generated by the maps

$$
e_A(G)=G(A),\qquad A\in\mathscr X.
$$

It is the smallest sigma-field that makes every $G\mapsto G(A)$ measurable.
On common spaces such as $\mathbb R^d$, one often equips
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ with the weak topology and uses its Borel sigma-field;
under standard conditions these constructions agree for the usual purposes.

Unpack the evaluation map as follows. Fix one data-space event $A$. Each
candidate distribution $G$ assigns it a number $G(A)\in[0,1]$. Thus

$$
e_A:G\longmapsto G(A)
$$

is an ordinary function whose inputs happen to be entire probability
measures. The evaluation sigma-field ensures that questions about these
numbers can be assigned prior probabilities.

The sentence about weak topology is optional on a first reading. A
**topology** is a formal rule for which points count as nearby and what
convergence means. The weak topology declares distributions close when they
give similar integrals for bounded continuous functions. The
[consistency note](posterior-consistency.qmd#weak-neighborhoods) explains this
without requiring a topology course.

Now a prior

$$
\Pi:\mathscr E\longrightarrow[0,1]
$$

is a probability measure on
$(\mathcal P(\mathcal X),\mathscr E)$.

# A random probability measure {#rpm-definition}

On an underlying probability space
$(\Omega_*,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$, a random probability measure is a measurable
map

$$
G:\Omega_*\longrightarrow\mathcal P(\mathcal X).
$$

Equivalently, for each measurable $A\subseteq\mathcal X$, the quantity $G(A)$
is a $[0,1]$-valued random variable, with compatibility across sets so that
each realized $G$ is a probability measure.

The star on $\Omega_*$ merely distinguishes the source of randomness used to
draw $G$ from the data space $\mathcal X$. Practically, the definition says:

1. before the draw, every $G(A)$ is uncertain;
2. one draw supplies probabilities for all events $A$ simultaneously;
3. the resulting set function obeys the probability axioms.

The law of this random object is

$$
\Pi(B)=\mathbb P(G\in B),
\qquad B\in\mathscr E.
$$

Thus the phrases

- “draw $G\sim\Pi$,”
- “put prior $\Pi$ on $G$,” and
- “$G$ is a random probability measure with law $\Pi$”

describe the same two-level construction.

## A random measure as a stochastic process {#rpm-stochastic-process}

For every data-space event $A$, the evaluation $G(A)$ is an ordinary random
variable. The indexed collection

$$
\{G(A):A\in\mathscr X\}
$$

can therefore be viewed as a **stochastic process indexed by sets**. A
stochastic process is simply a compatible collection of random variables with
an index telling us which component is being examined. Here the index is an
event $A$, rather than time.

The compatibility condition is crucial. Arbitrarily assigning unrelated
random variables to different sets would not ensure that one realization
$A\mapsto G(A)$ is countably additive and has total mass one.

The more general term **random measure** does not require total mass one. For
example, a spatial point process may assign a random count $N(A)$ to each
region $A$. A random probability measure is the special case in which every
realization has nonnegative mass and $G(\mathcal X)=1$.

# The notation at the two levels {#rpm-two-level-notation}

For a measurable function $h$ on the data space,

$$
\int_{\mathcal X}h(x)G(dx)
$$

integrates over possible **data values** under a particular distribution $G$.

For a functional $T$ of a distribution,

$$
\int_{\mathcal P(\mathcal X)}T(G)\Pi(dG)
$$

integrates over possible **distributions** under the prior.

A **functional** is a function whose input is an entire distribution. For
example, $T(G)=G(A)$, $T(G)=\int xG(dx)$, and a median of $G$ are all
functionals.

| Expression | Varying object | Integrating measure |
|---|---|---|
| $\int h(x)G(dx)$ | Data value $x$ | Candidate sampling distribution $G$ |
| $\int T(G)\Pi(dG)$ | Entire distribution $G$ | Prior law $\Pi$ |
| $\int G(A)\Pi(dG)$ | Entire distribution $G$ | Prior law $\Pi$ |

The last expression is the prior mean probability assigned to $A$.

# Random probability measures outside Bayesian priors {#rpm-non-bayesian-examples}

Not every random probability measure represents prior uncertainty about an
unknown population law. The empirical distribution is a basic
repeated-sampling example:

$$
\widehat P_n
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}.
$$

For a realized dataset, $\widehat P_n$ is one fixed probability measure. Before
the data are observed, it is random because its support points
$X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are random. For every measurable $A$,

$$
\widehat P_n(A)
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1(X_i\in A)
$$

is the random sample proportion falling in $A$. Its law on
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ is induced by the repeated-sampling distribution of
the data, not by a Bayesian prior.

The ordinary nonparametric bootstrap supplies another example. Conditional on
the observed data,

$$
\widehat P_n^*
=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{N_i}{n}\delta_{X_i},
$$

where the counts have a multinomial distribution. The bootstrap measure is
random because its weights are random. This resembles a Bayesian-bootstrap
draw computationally, but its inferential interpretation is different.

These examples show that “random probability measure” names a mathematical
type of random object. A prior, posterior, empirical measure, or bootstrap
law can each produce that type for a different reason.

# Parametric Bayes also induces a prior on distributions {#rpm-parametric-induced-prior}

Suppose

$$
X\mid\theta\sim P_\theta,
\qquad
\theta\sim\pi.
$$

The map $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ pushes the prior $\pi$ forward to a law
$\Pi$ on $\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$:

$$
\Pi(B)=\pi\{\theta:P_\theta\in B\}.
$$

This is the same pushforward construction as $P_X=P\circ X^{-1}$. The input
map now takes a parameter value $\theta$ to an entire distribution
$P_\theta$. See the [pushforward explanation](sets-functions-and-pushforwards.qmd#why-it-is-called-a-pushforward).

So Walker is correct that a parametric Bayesian can also be viewed as placing a
prior on sampling distributions. The distinction is support:

- a fixed $p$-dimensional parametric model restricts $G$ to
  $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p\}$;
- a nonparametric prior is not confined to one fixed finite-dimensional
  family.

“Nonparametric” does **not** mean that every distribution receives positive
prior probability. Priors on infinite-dimensional spaces still have support
restrictions.

Informally, the **support** is the collection of possibilities the prior does
not rule out, including limiting possibilities that may have zero probability
individually. A precise neighborhood definition appears in the
[posterior-consistency note](posterior-consistency.qmd#prior-support).

# Densities versus probability measures {#rpm-densities-vs-measures}

If all candidates $G$ are dominated by a common measure $\lambda$, write

$$
f=\frac{dG}{d\lambda}.
$$

Then one may work with a space $\mathcal D$ of densities and write the prior as
$\Pi(df)$. In that setting, $f$ is a realization of a random density.

This representation is convenient but not universal:

- a probability measure need not have a density relative to Lebesgue measure;
- a Dirichlet-process draw is usually discrete;
- mixed and singular distributions are naturally represented as measures.

Here **singular** means concentrated on a set having Lebesgue measure zero,
as a point mass is concentrated on one point. The
[Dirac note](dirac-measure-and-dirac-delta.qmd#dirac-not-lebesgue-density)
gives the basic example.

Use $G$ or $F$ when the random object is a probability measure and $f$ when it
is specifically a density relative to a stated dominating measure.

# A finite random-measure example {#rpm-finite-example}

Fix points $x_1,\ldots,x_K$ and draw random weights

$$
(W_1,\ldots,W_K)\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_K).
$$

Define

$$
G=\sum_{k=1}^K W_k\delta_{x_k}.
$$

For every measurable $A$,

$$
G(A)=\sum_{k=1}^K W_k\mathbf 1(x_k\in A).
$$

Each draw of the weights yields an entire probability measure. The law of the
weight vector induces a law $\Pi$ on probability measures. This finite example
already contains the essential logic of a random probability measure.

# The Dirichlet process {#rpm-dirichlet-process}

Ferguson's Dirichlet process is a probability law on probability measures
[@ferguson1973dp]. Write

$$
G\sim\operatorname{DP}(\alpha,H),
$$

where $\alpha>0$ is a concentration parameter and $H$ is a base probability
measure. Its defining property is that for every finite measurable partition
$A_1,\ldots,A_K$ of $\mathcal X$,

$$
\{G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_K)\}
\sim
\operatorname{Dirichlet}
\{\alpha H(A_1),\ldots,\alpha H(A_K)\}.
\tag{1}
$$

Equation (1) specifies a consistent collection of finite-dimensional
distributions for the random measure.

A **partition** consists of nonoverlapping sets whose union is the whole
space. The DP statement says: choose any finite way to divide the data space;
the vector of random probabilities assigned to those pieces has a Dirichlet
distribution. “Consistent” means that splitting a piece more finely or joining
pieces back together gives compatible probability statements, so all such
finite vectors can describe one random measure $G$.

Consequences include

$$
E\{G(A)\}=H(A),
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}\{G(A)\}
=\frac{H(A)\{1-H(A)\}}{\alpha+1}.
$$

Larger $\alpha$ concentrates $G$ more tightly around $H$.

Even when $H$ is continuous, a DP draw $G$ is almost surely discrete. A
stick-breaking representation makes this visible:

$$
G=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}W_j\delta_{\Theta_j}.
$$

Here $W_j\geq0$ and $\sum_jW_j=1$, while $\Theta_j$ are random locations.
Thus one draw is a countable weighted collection of point masses. The
[applied DP-mixture note](../Bayesian/bayes-nonpar-concept-applied.qmd#stick-breaking-representation)
shows how the weights are generated.

This fact is not a defect. In density estimation, $G$ is commonly used as a
random **mixing distribution**.

“Almost surely” means with probability one under the randomness that draws
$G$; exceptional draws may exist mathematically but have probability zero.
See [null sets and almost surely](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd#null-sets-almost-everywhere-and-almost-surely).

# A DP mixture produces a random density {#rpm-dp-mixture}

Let $k(x\mid\theta)$ be a kernel density and let

$$
G\sim\operatorname{DP}(\alpha,H).
$$

Define

$$
f_G(x)=\int k(x\mid\theta)G(d\theta).
$$

If $G=\sum_jW_j\delta_{\Theta_j}$, then

$$
f_G(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}W_jk(x\mid\Theta_j).
$$

Thus

- $G$ is discrete on parameter space;
- $f_G$ can be a smooth continuous density on data space;
- the law of $G$ induces a prior on the random density $f_G$.

This is the distinction between a **Dirichlet process prior** and a
**Dirichlet-process mixture model**.

# Prior predictive and posterior predictive distributions {#rpm-prediction}

Suppose

$$
G\sim\Pi,
\qquad
X_i\mid G\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim G.
$$

Before data, the predictive probability of $A$ is

$$
P(X_1\in A)=\int G(A)\Pi(dG).
$$

After observing $X_{1:n}$, let $\Pi_n$ be the posterior law of $G$. Then

$$
P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid X_{1:n})
=\int G(A)\Pi_n(dG).
\tag{2}
$$

Equation (2) is the posterior mean of the random measure $G$. If every $G$ has density
$f$, its density version is

$$
f_n(x)=\int f(x)\Pi_n(df).
$$

The predictive distribution averages sampling distributions under current
posterior uncertainty. It is not generally the same as evaluating the model at
a posterior mean parameter.

# Connection to exchangeability {#rpm-exchangeability}

Conditional iid sampling gives the joint law

$$
P(X_1\in A_1,\ldots,X_n\in A_n)
=\int\prod_{i=1}^n G(A_i)\Pi(dG).
$$

This expression is unchanged by permuting observation labels, so the sequence
is exchangeable. Representation theorems of de Finetti and Hewitt-Savage give
a converse under appropriate conditions: an infinitely exchangeable sequence
can be represented as conditionally iid given a random directing probability
measure [@hewitt1955symmetric].

**Exchangeable** means that the joint distribution is unchanged if subject
labels are permuted. It is weaker than marginal independence: after $G$ is
integrated out, observations are usually dependent because they share the
same uncertain $G$.

# Three distinctions to keep visible {#rpm-three-levels}

| Object | Example | What it assigns probability to |
|---|---|---|
| Sampling distribution | $G$ | Subsets of data space $\mathcal X$ |
| Prior/posterior law | $\Pi$ or $\Pi_n$ | Sets of candidate distributions $G$ |
| Predictive distribution | $\int G\,d\Pi_n$ | Subsets of data space after averaging over posterior uncertainty |

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. Which object assigns a probability to the event $X\in A$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

For a fixed candidate sampling distribution $G$, the answer is $G(A)$; $G$
lives on data space. If $G$ is still uncertain and is averaged under a prior or
posterior, the corresponding predictive probability is
$\int G(A)\Pi(dG)$ or $\int G(A)\Pi_n(dG)$.
:::

**2. Which object assigns a probability to a set of candidate distributions?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The prior $\Pi$ (or posterior $\Pi_n$) does. It is a probability measure on the
model space $\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ equipped with its sigma-field $\mathscr E$.
Thus $\Pi(B)$ is defined when $B$ is a measurable set of candidate
distributions.
:::

**3. Why is a parametric prior also a prior on distributions?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Each parameter value $\theta$ determines a sampling distribution $P_\theta$.
Pushing the parameter prior $\pi$ through the map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ gives

$$
\Pi(B)=\pi\{\theta:P_\theta\in B\}.
$$

The induced $\Pi$ is a prior on distributions, although its support is confined
to the parametric family $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$.
:::

**4. Does a DP draw from a continuous base measure have a continuous density?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. Even when the base measure $H$ is continuous, a Dirichlet-process draw is
almost surely discrete: it is a countable weighted sum of Dirac measures. It
therefore generally has no density with respect to Lebesgue measure. Do not
confuse the draw $G$ with the density $f_G$ produced by a DP **mixture**.
:::

**5. How can a discrete random mixing measure generate a continuous sampling
density?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

For $G=\sum_jW_j\delta_{\Theta_j}$ and a continuous density kernel,

$$
f_G(x)=\int k(x\mid\theta)G(d\theta)
=\sum_jW_jk(x\mid\Theta_j).
$$

$G$ is discrete on parameter space, while each $k(\,·\mid\Theta_j)$ spreads
mass continuously over data space. Their weighted sum can therefore be a
continuous density.
:::

**6. Why is the empirical distribution a random probability measure before
the data are observed?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

For every realized sample,

$$
\widehat P_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}
$$

is a probability measure. Before sampling, its locations $X_i$ are random, so
the entire measure $\widehat P_n$ is a random element of
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$. Its randomness comes from the sampling law, not from
a prior on the unknown population distribution.
:::
